::: {#exm-mse-sample-mean}
#### Population mean squared error of two estimators of a population mean

Continuing @exm-bias-sample-mean,
suppose also that $\dsn{X}$ are mutually independent,
each with variance $\Var{\Rvar_\iobs} = \varpar$.
Both $\bar X$ and $X_1$ have zero bias,
so by @thm-mse-bias-variance each estimator's pMSE
equals its variance.

For $X_1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \pMSE{X_1} &= 0^2 + \Var{X_1} \\
  &= \varpar.
\end{aligned}
$$

For $\bar X$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pMSE{\bar X}
&= \sqf{\bias{\bar X}} + \Var{\bar X}
&& \text{(pMSE equals bias squared plus variance)}\\
&= 0^2 + \Var{\bar X}
&& \text{(zero bias)}\\
&= \Var{\bar X}
&& \text{($0^2 = 0$)}\\
&= \Var{\avgin \Rvar_\iobs}
&& \text{(definition of $\bar X$)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2}\sumin \Var{\Rvar_\iobs}
&& \text{(variance of a linear combination of independent variables)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2}\sumin \varpar
&& \text{($\Var{\Rvar_\iobs} = \varpar$ for every $i$)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\varpar
&& \text{(sum of $n$ copies of $\varpar$)}\\
&= \frac{\varpar}{n}
&& \text{(cancel one factor of $n$)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The step to $\frac{1}{n^2}\sumin \Var{\Rvar_\iobs}$ uses
the [variance of a linear combination](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#thm-var-lincom),
whose covariance terms are all zero for independent variables.
The result $\varpar/n$ is the
[variance of an IID sample mean](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/limit-theorems.html#cor-mean-iid-moments).

So for any sample size $n > 1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \pMSE{\bar X} &= \varpar/n \\
  &< \varpar \\
  &= \pMSE{X_1}:
\end{aligned}
$$

by mean squared error, the sample mean is the more accurate estimator.
With $n = 50$ students, as in @exm-estimator,
the sample mean's mean squared error is $1/50$ of $X_1$'s.

:::
